## Introduction

If your OneNote second brain has grown to hundreds of notes across dozens
of sections, search starts to fail you. It is not that search does not
work — it is that it requires you to already know roughly *where* a note
lives. If you cannot remember the section, you get swamped with results
and spend time hunting. The mental overhead of maintaining a
location-based memory on top of the actual content defeats the purpose of
having a second brain at all.

This tutorial takes you from that notebook to a **clean Obsidian vault**:
plain markdown files you can search without remembering the folder,
navigate from index notes, and (optionally) hand to an AI agent without
re-explaining the whole project every session.

The [Obsidian Importer](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-importer)
will get the text across. It will not leave you with a usable vault. The
work is the cleanup: attachments, metadata, structure, and a handful of
index notes that turn a pile of files into something you can actually
move around in.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Why leave OneNote at all?

I wrote about consolidating notes into a second brain in my review of
[Building a Second Brain](/book-reviews/06-second-brain.qmd). OneNote
served that job for years. Two things eventually broke it.

**Search at scale.** A location-based notebook asks you to remember the
map as well as the content. At a few hundred notes that tax becomes the
main cost of using the system.

**Open files.** A vault of markdown is readable by any tool, any script,
any agent with filesystem access. OneNote's proprietary format and closed
API make that basically impossible. That openness is what the last
section of this tutorial is for.
:::

### Intended audience

People with a **large OneNote notebook** who want to land in a clean,
usable Obsidian vault. You do not need prior Obsidian experience. You
should be comfortable installing a desktop app, signing into a Microsoft
account, and moving files on your computer.

If you already live in Obsidian and only want the agent-oriented
conventions, skip to [Make it agent-ready](#make-it-agent-ready).

### What you'll need

- [ ] [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/) desktop (not only the mobile app)
- [ ] The notebook you want to migrate, available in OneNote via a
  **Microsoft account** (the Importer talks to Microsoft's API, not to
  local `.one` files)
- [ ] A **backup** of that notebook — copy it, or at least confirm it
  still lives in OneNote until you trust the vault
- [ ] A spare hour for a medium notebook; a large one will take longer
  because you will export in phases
- [ ] Optional: a terminal and a text editor that can search-and-replace
  across a folder (VS Code, Cursor, or similar). Useful once you have
  hundreds of files; not required to follow the path

You do not need Claude Code, Dataview, or git to finish. Those show up
later as accelerators.

## Export in phases

1. Create a new vault in Obsidian. Use an empty folder. Do not import
   into a vault you already care about until you have practised on a
   copy.
2. Settings → Community plugins → turn off Restricted mode → Browse →
   install **Importer**. Enable it.
3. Open the Importer command (`Importer: Open importer`) and choose
   **OneNote**. Sign into the Microsoft account that holds the notebook.
4. Export **one section, or one small notebook, at a time** rather than
   the entire second brain in one go.

Phased export is the difference between a complete dump and a stalled
one. The Microsoft Graph API will throttle or time out on a large
notebook. In my case the full vault was hundreds of notes across dozens
of sections; running the export in several passes was the only way to
get everything across.

When a phase finishes, glance at the target folder. You should see
markdown files nested under something like `OneNote/<Notebook name>/`,
plus a pile of image files. If a section comes through empty, run that
section again before moving on.

::: {.callout-tip}
Keep OneNote available until you have finished the cleanup and used the
vault for a week. The importer is a copy, not a cut. You are allowed to
go back.
:::

## Recognise a raw import

Before you tidy anything, walk the vault and write down what you see.
The importer's job is text. Everything else is leftover OneNote
structure. A raw dump typically looks like this — these numbers are from
my vault, so you can calibrate; yours will differ.

- **Image files dumped at the vault root.** I had 672, with no folder
  of their own.
- **Frontmatter that is not useful yet.** Every note carried an
  `onenote-id` and nothing else: no tags, no dates, no aliases.
- **Almost no knowledge graph.** I had one genuine cross-note wikilink
  in the entire vault. OneNote sections do not become Obsidian links.
- **Formatting noise.** Escaped angle brackets (`\<like this\>`),
  `==highlight==` markers from the export, numbered lists that no longer
  number.
- **Empty stub notes.** Pages that existed in OneNote but had no body
  (19 in my dump, plus a few directories that only existed to hold
  them).
- **A redundant path prefix.** Everything nested under
  `OneNote/2nd Brain/`, so the real topic folders sat two levels too
  deep.
- **No Obsidian-native structure.** No tags, no templates, no Daily
  Notes configuration pointing at the dated notes you already have.

Open Graph view now. It will look sparse: a cloud of unlinked dots, maybe
a couple of accidental links. That is the "before" in the video at the
top of this page. You are not done until that view has hubs.

Make a short checklist from *your* dump before you change files. The
next two sections are easier if you know whether you have 20 images or
700.

::: {.callout-warning}
Work on a **copy of the vault folder** until the cleanup looks right.
Moving and deleting notes is hard to undo if you have not yet put the
vault in git.
:::

## Immediate fixes

Do the mechanical work first. None of it requires judgement about how
you think; it just stops the vault from being unpleasant to open.

### Put attachments in one folder

Create an `attachments/` folder at the vault root and move the image
files into it. Obsidian resolves wikilink embeds by filename across the
vault, so `![[some-image.png]]` keeps working — you do not have to edit
every note.

In the system file browser that is a select-and-move. From a terminal,
something like:

```bash
mkdir -p attachments
mv *.png *.jpg *.jpeg *.gif *.webp attachments/ 2>/dev/null
```

Adjust the glob if your importer used different extensions. Spot-check a
note that embeds an image before you continue.

### Strip export artefacts

Search the vault for `\<` and `\>`. In my dump that was 1,101 backslash
escapes across 118 files. Replace `\<` with `<` and `\>` with `>`.

Obsidian's search can find them; a folder-wide replace in a text editor
is faster once you have confirmed the pattern is really an export
artefact and not a code snippet you meant to keep. Then search for
`==` and decide whether to keep highlight markers or turn them into
plain bold / nothing.

Numbered lists that restart at `1.` on every line are a similar pass:
fix them when you next edit that note, or tidy the worst files now.

### Delete empty stubs

Open notes that have no body — often only the `onenote-id` frontmatter.
If they were accidental OneNote pages, delete them. If they were
placeholders you still want, leave them and give them a one-line
description so they stop looking like importer debris.

After deleting, remove any folders that are now empty.

### Flatten the path prefix

If every topic folder sits under `OneNote/<Notebook name>/`, move those
topic folders up to the vault root. In my vault that meant 13 top-level
folders sitting directly in the vault, instead of two extra layers of
"I used to be a notebook."

Rename in Obsidian rather than the system file browser if you have
already created any wikilinks — see [automatic link
updating](#turn-on-automatic-link-updating) below, and turn that setting
on before you move things.

## Structure

The vault should now open without a junk drawer of images at the root.
Next you give notes metadata Obsidian (and later, you) can filter on.

### Folder-derived tags

Pick a tagging rule and apply it everywhere, including notes you have
not opened yet. The rule I used: **each folder segment becomes a tag**,
kebab-cased, with noise words dropped.

Examples from my vault:

- `Developer/LLMs/` → `[developer, llm]`
- `Ai Justice Unit/Magic-Mail/` → `[ai-justice, magic-mail]`

That produced 38 tag combinations across 420 notes. The exact vocabulary
matters less than consistency. An agent, or future you, should be able
to filter `[ai-justice, magic-mail]` and get that project without the
rest of the vault attached.

Replace the `onenote-id` field while you are in the frontmatter. It is
not something you will search for. A note ends up looking like this:

```yaml
---
tags:
  - developer
  - llm
---
```

For a handful of folders you can do this by hand. For hundreds of notes,
a small script or an agent with filesystem access is a reasonable
accelerator — you are applying a rule, not composing prose. Either way,
**you** decide the tag set; do not let a tool invent a parallel
vocabulary.

### Point Daily Notes at the notes you already have

If OneNote (or your own habit) already produced dated notes, do not
invent a second daily-note scheme. Configure the Daily Notes core plugin
to match what you have.

Mine lived at `TODO/YYYY.MM.DD`. The settings that made them navigable:

- **Date format** matching the filename (`YYYY.MM.DD` in my case)
- **New file location** set to that folder (`TODO`)

Install the community **Calendar** plugin so those dates appear in the
sidebar. I had 74 daily notes that went from "files in a folder" to
"click the date" once this was set.

If you do not have dated notes yet, you can skip this and add Daily
Notes later. Do not create empty dailies just to fill the calendar.

### Turn on automatic link updating

Settings → Files and links → **Automatically update internal links**.
With this on, renaming or moving a note in Obsidian rewrites every
wikilink that pointed at it. Turn it on before the next section, where
you will create index notes and will want to rename things without
breaking them.

## Navigation

A vault of tagged markdown is still a pile of files until it has entry
points. Maps of Content (MOCs) are ordinary notes that link out to
everything in a section. They are the hubs in the graph video.

### Create MOC notes in the richest folders

You do not need an MOC for every folder. Start with the sections that
already have a lot of notes.

1. In that folder, create a note named `_MOC.md` (the underscore keeps
   it at the top of the file list).
2. Add a short heading and a wikilink to every note in the folder.
3. Repeat for the next dense section.

I ended up with 10 MOCs, in places like `Developer/LLMs/_MOC.md` and
`Ai Justice Unit/Justice Transcribe/_MOC.md`. Each one is both a human
table of contents and a graph-view hub: one node with many edges, instead
of a cloud of orphans.

A minimal MOC looks like this:

```markdown
# LLMs

- [[some-model-notes]]
- [[prompt-patterns]]
- [[eval-gotchas]]
```

You can generate the link list with a file listing and a bit of editing.
The value is the *existence* of the hub, not a perfect taxonomy on day
one.

### Confirm the graph

Open Graph view. You should now see clusters around each `_MOC` — the
"after" in the video at the top of this page. If a section you care
about is still a scatter of unlinked dots, it needs an MOC (or a few
wikilinks between notes that actually relate).

The Calendar plugin in the sidebar is the other navigation surface:
daily notes by date, MOCs by topic.

## Make it agent-ready

Plain markdown is the reason this vault is more useful than the OneNote
notebook you started with. An agent with filesystem access can read,
search, and write notes directly — no proprietary format, no API, no
export step. Tags and MOCs are how that agent orients without opening
every file.

The steps below are what I would do on a vault I expected to share with
a teammate or with Claude Code. Do them on yours once the structure
above feels stable.

### Add a `VAULT.md` at the root

This is the first file an agent should read, and a useful orientation
note for humans too. It is the vault equivalent of a `CLAUDE.md` in a
code repository: a single entry point that explains the map.

Include:

- what the top-level folders are and what belongs in each
- the tagging convention you actually use
- where daily notes live and how they are named
- where the MOCs are
- anything an agent must not do (for example: do not delete notes, do
  not rewrite history)

### Add `_PROJECT.md` notes for active work

For each live project, keep a structured state note — current status,
key decisions, open questions, links to the relevant notes and people.
That is the highest-value context to hand an agent (or yourself) at the
start of a session. Name them consistently (`_PROJECT.md` in the project
folder, or a single `Projects/` folder with one note per effort) so they
are findable.

Daily notes then become the temporal log. An agent can read the last
handful of dailies to see what moved recently, instead of needing a
recap.

### Put the vault in git

A private remote beats relying solely on Obsidian Sync if you care about
history you can diff. Markdown merge conflicts are readable; OneNote
ones are not.

A sensible starting `.gitignore`:

```gitignore
.obsidian/workspace.json
.obsidian/workspace-mobile.json
.obsidian/graph.json
.trash/
```

Commit the rest of `.obsidian/` if you want plugin lists and settings to
travel with the vault. Push to a **private** remote.

Meaningful commit messages ("Added notes from Docker workshop") give you
a changelog. Do not expect 47 auto-saves to be useful later.

### Keep tagging as you go

The folder-derived tags only help if new notes get them. When you create
a note in `Developer/LLMs/`, give it `[developer, llm]` in the same
motion. Inconsistent tags are how the filter becomes noisy again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Optional stretch (not required to finish)

**`created` dates in frontmatter.** Agents (and you) can reason about
recency. A 2024 note about a deprecated tool is less relevant than
something from last week. You can backfill from file modification times
as a rough approximation.

**Dataview.** Once enough notes are tagged, the Dataview community
plugin can generate lists inside a note ("all `[ai-justice]` notes
modified in the last 30 days"). Those dynamic summaries are compact
context for humans and for agents. Install it after the tagging
convention is stable, not before.
:::

## Wrap-up

You should now have:

- a vault of markdown, not a OneNote notebook
- attachments in one place
- tags you can filter on, instead of `onenote-id`
- Daily Notes (if you had dated pages) wired to the Calendar
- MOC notes, and a graph that looks like it has a shape
- optionally, a `VAULT.md`, project state notes, and git history

What you can do that you could not do in OneNote: search without already
knowing the section; rename a note without breaking the map; point an
agent at a folder and have it read the same files you do.

This is not a PKM theory piece, and it is not an Obsidian plugin
catalogue. The migration overhead is real, but it is a one-time cost.
The combination of structured markdown, consistent tagging, navigable
MOCs, and git history is what makes the vault worth the afternoon.
